message.content:
The term “great schisms” is often used to refer to the most consequential splits in Christian history that reshaped the religious landscape. While there are many divisions, three stand out for their lasting impact:

| # | Schism | Approximate Year | Key Parties | Main Causes | Consequences |
|---|--------|------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| **1** | **Great Schism (East–West Schism)** | 1054 | Eastern Orthodox Church vs. Roman Catholic Church | Doctrinal differences (e.g., Filioque clause), political tensions, cultural divergence, disputes over papal authority | Formal split into Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism; long‑lasting theological and liturgical differences |
| **2** | **Protestant Reformation** | 1517–1648 | Various European Protestant groups (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, Anabaptist, etc.) vs. Roman Catholic Church | Corruption in the Church, desire for doctrinal reform, printing press dissemination, political opportunism | Emergence of numerous Protestant denominations; Counter‑Reformation; religious wars; shift toward modern nation‑states |
| **3** | **East–West Schism (also called the Schism of 1054)** | 1054 | Same as above | See Great Schism | See Great Schism |

> **Note:** The Great Schism and the East–West Schism refer to the same event; it’s sometimes listed twice because it’s considered both a “schism” and a “great schism.” Some scholars also include the **East–West Schism** as a separate entry due to its profound influence on Eastern Christianity.

These three events—often grouped together as the “great schisms”—are the most widely recognized and studied divisions in Christian history.
